Issued at 530 AM CDT Mon Sep 7 2026

Upper level synoptic features early this morning include a deep
longwave trough over the western CONUS with an embedded double-
circulation closed low spinning through the Pacific Northwest 
and a downstream ridge tilting positively from Texas to the 
Upper Mississippi River Valley. At the surface, lee troughing 
is analyzed from southern Saskatchewan through the Foothills of
Colorado. A nocturnal low level jet is supplying warm air 
advection and moisture transport through the western Dakotas, 
which is responsible for clusters of showers and thunderstorms 
early this morning. A shortwave has ejected from the base of the
longwave trough into eastern Montana, and associated height 
falls should contribute to an areal increase of showers storms 
along the ND/MT border by mid morning. Model guidance is in good
agreement that 700-500 mb DCVA will drive a broad corridor of 
showers and thunderstorms over a stable but very moist boundary 
layer from western North Dakota around mid morning to eastern 
North Dakota in the mid to late afternoon. This initial round 
of convection is likely to remain elevated, but steep mid level 
lapse rates and modest to high deep layer RH above the base of 
the EML could yield up to 1000-2000 J/kg of CAPE. Effective bulk
shear is forecast to vary over space and time, but generally 
remains in the 30-50 kt range, sufficient for severe storms. 
CAMs favor a cluster or linear mode with the initial round on 
account of the strong forcing and lack of underlying surface 
boundary. But the stable boundary layer could mitigate the risk 
for damaging winds to some extent. 

This afternoon, the upper low closest to the base of the 
longwave trough will pivot northeastward into western Montana 
and form a separate mid level double-circulation low with the 
lead shortwave. This process should begin driving the lee 
surface trough eastward, with a rapidly occluding cyclone over 
southeast Saskatchewan by this evening. How the initial round 
of storms plays out this morning and early afternoon lowers 
confidence in the mesoscale environment in the western half of 
North Dakota later this afternoon. But if strong diurnal heating
occurs, a corridor of up to 2000 J/kg of SBCAPE with little to 
no CIN could develop along and just ahead of the surface trough.
Strong low level convergence along the trough could be 
coincident with a corridor of 850 mb warm air advection. This, 
with continued height falls in a southwest flow regime, could 
provide enough forcing for convective initiation in the western 
half of the state later this afternoon. This second round of 
convection is more likely to be discrete with only isolated to 
widely scattered coverage at most. But these storms would carry 
a much higher threat ceiling, including a tornado risk 
supported by strong low level shear and low LCLs. Model 
hodographs show strong streamwise vorticity in the 0-l km layer
and would support splitting supercells. There is still a chance
though that all these ingredients will not become properly 
aligned. Therefore, have not made any deviations from our 
forecast hazards at golf ball size hail, 70 mph wind, and a 
conditional risk for a tornado.

Any thunderstorm throughout the day could be a very prolific 
rain producer with anomalously high precipitable water around 
1.5-1.75". Extrapolation of early morning convection paired with
rapid refresh guidance suggests the highest probability for 
training convection is across northwest and north central North 
Dakota from around sunrise to midday.

One final day of unseasonably humid conditions today, with the 
southwest becoming drier in the afternoon as the lee trough 
pushes in. Forecast highs range from the mid 70s northeast to 
upper 80s southwest. The surface trough will transition to more 
of a traditional cold or occluded front this evening, and 
trailing strong low to mid level dry slotting should put an end 
to any isolated storms that persist beyond early evening. There 
is some concern that the deepening cyclone over southern 
Saskatchewan could bring a corridor of very strong winds into 
northwest North Dakota late this evening through tonight, but 
model soundings show just enough of a surface inversion to 
prevent maximum potential momentum transfer of up to 50 kts. 
The strong cyclone will spin into southwest Manitoba on Tuesday,
bringing cooler temperatures and strong westerly winds across 
the state. Confidence remains high in sustained winds around 30 
to 35 mph with gusts to around 50 mph. Barring any last-minute 
forecast deviations, a Wind Advisory will likely be needed for 
most, if not all parts of our forecast area. Forecast highs on
